**Hello, I’m [Your Name], a perinatal mental‑health specialist.**  
I’m here to support you as you navigate the early weeks of motherhood. Today we’ll be using the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)** – a brief, well‑validated questionnaire that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling over the past week.  

The EPDS is not a diagnostic tool; it simply gives us a clearer picture of any mood, anxiety, or stress symptoms you may be experiencing. Everything you share is completely confidential, and this is a safe space where you can speak openly without judgment.  

We’ll go through **10 short questions**, one at a time, and I’ll listen to your responses. There’s no right or wrong answer—just answer how you truly feel.  

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin.

**First question:**  
*In the past seven days, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things?*
I’ve hardly ever felt like I could laugh or see the funny side of things in the past week.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Actually, I haven’t really been able to laugh or see the funny side of things much lately.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I’ve hardly ever felt that way—I don’t really look forward to things or feel much enjoyment right now.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Yes, I find myself blaming myself unnecessarily when things go wrong—I feel guilty and often think I’m not doing enough as a mother.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, I’ve been feeling anxious and worried a lot lately, even about things that don’t seem to have a real reason. It’s especially about my baby’s health and safety, and the worries just keep circling in my head.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Yes, I’ve felt scared and even panicky at times for no clear reason, and it just adds to the anxiety I’m already feeling.
Things have been getting on top of me

I’ve been feeling like everything is just piling up on me. Even simple tasks feel overwhelming, and I’m constantly worried that I’m not handling things well enough. It’s hard to keep up, and I often feel like I’m barely managing.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes, I’ve been feeling really unhappy most days, and it’s been hard to fall asleep or stay asleep. I wake up many times during the night and it takes a long time to get back to sleep, which just leaves me feeling even more exhausted.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yes, I’ve been feeling sad and miserable most days.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Yes, I’ve found myself crying a few times this week when I feel especially overwhelmed or sad.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

I’m really sorry you’re feeling this way. It sounds like you’re in a lot of pain right now, and it’s important to reach out for help right away. Please consider calling your local emergency services (for example, 911 in the United States) or going to your nearest emergency department. You can also call a suicide prevention hotline right now:

- **United States:** 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) – available 24/7, free and confidential  
- **United Kingdom:** 116 123 (Samaritans) – free 24/7  
- **Canada:** 1‑833‑456‑4566 (Talk Suicide) – 24/7, toll‑free  
- **Australia:** 13 11 14 (Lifeline) – 24/7, free  

If you’re outside these countries, you can find international hotlines here: https://findahelpline.com/, or you can search online for “suicide helpline” plus the name of your country.

If you have a mental‑health professional you’ve seen before, please let them know what’s happening as soon as possible. If you can, tell a trusted friend, family member, or partner about how you’re feeling so they can help you get the support you need right away.

You don’t have to go through this alone—people do want to help you, and there are resources and professionals ready to support you right now. Please reach out for help immediately.

I hear how overwhelming and painful this time has been for you-feeling unable to laugh, lacking enjoyment, experiencing intense guilt, constant worry, panic, sleeplessness, sadness, frequent crying, and thoughts of harming yourself. You are not alone, and it's understandable to feel exhausted and frightened while caring for your baby.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports hardly ever feeling enjoyment or looking forward to things, matching the 'Hardly at all' option.</sym>, <sym>The response indicates frequent self‑blame and guilt, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, pervasive anxiety and worry, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling scared/panicky at times, matching 'Yes, sometimes' option</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelming feelings and inability to cope, matching 'Yes, most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling unhappy most days with frequent sleep problems, matching 'Yes, most of the time' option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling sad and miserable most days, matching 'Yes, most of the time' option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying a few times this week, matching 'Only occasionally' option.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** The patient's responses indicate high scores on all EPDS items, yielding a total of 23, which exceeds the ≥14 threshold for probable postpartum depression and triggers an urgent referral per EPDS guidelines. Reported <sym>anhedonia</sym> (<quote>I haven't really been able to laugh or see the funny side of things</quote>), <sym>persistent sadness</sym> (<quote>I've been feeling sad and miserable most days</quote>), <sym>excessive guilt</sym> (<quote>I feel guilty and often think I'm not doing enough as a mother</quote>), <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic</sym> (<quote>I've been feeling anxious and worried a lot lately</quote>), <sym>sleep disturbance</sym> (<quote>It's been hard to fall asleep or stay asleep</quote>), and <sym>suicidal thoughts</sym> are present, meeting several core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> in the DSM‑5 (depressed mood, loss of interest, guilt, insomnia, fatigue, diminished concentration, recurrent thoughts of death). The combination of functional impairment, pervasive dysphoria, and self‑harm ideation warrants immediate safety assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Contact emergency services or a crisis hotline immediately due to suicidal thoughts
2. Arrange an urgent appointment with a <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
3. Develop a safety plan with a trusted support person and limit access to means of self‑harm
4. Implement sleep hygiene practices, such as a consistent bedtime routine and limiting screen time before sleep
5. Begin regular mood monitoring and consider evidence‑based psychotherapy such as CBT or interpersonal therapy for postpartum depression
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: **Postpartum Mood & Anxiety Screening – Summary**

**Client Identifier:** [Redacted]  
**Date of Screening:** [Insert Date]  
**Clinician:** [Licensed Mental Health Professional]  

---

### 1. Reported Symptoms & Emotional/Behavioral Concerns
| Domain | Patient Report |
|--------|----------------|
| **Anhedonia / Low Mood** | Inability to laugh or see humor; little enjoyment or anticipation of activities; persistent sadness and feeling “miserable.” |
| **Guilt / Self‑Blame** | Frequent unnecessary self‑blame; feeling guilty and “not doing enough” as a mother. |
| **Anxiety / Worry** | Persistent anxiety and worry without clear trigger, especially regarding infant’s health and safety; feeling “scared” or “panicky” without obvious reason. |
| **Overwhelm / Stress** | Tasks feel overwhelming; sense that everything is “piling up”; difficulty coping with daily demands. |
| **Sleep Disturbance** | Difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, frequent nocturnal awakenings; resulting exhaustion. |
| **Crying / Tearfulness** | Crying episodes several times per week, typically when feeling overwhelmed or sad. |
| **Suicidal Ideation** | Patient indicated thoughts of self‑harm (see response to Q10). |

---

### 2. Consistent Patterns Across Responses
- **Low mood & loss of pleasure** (Q1‑Q3, Q8‑Q9).  
- **Elevated anxiety & panic symptoms** (Q4‑Q5).  
- **Excessive self‑criticism/guilt** (Q3).  
- **Feeling overwhelmed and unable to manage responsibilities** (Q6).  
- **Sleep disruption associated with dysphoric mood** (Q7).  
- **Presence of suicidal thoughts** (Q10).

---

### 3. Areas of Screening Significance (Postpartum Context)
- **Postpartum Depression:** Anhedonia, persistent sadness, crying, guilt, sleep disturbance, functional impairment.  
- **Postpartum Anxiety:** Excessive worry about infant health, panic‑type symptoms, feeling “on edge.”  
- **Postpartum PTSD / Trauma (screening):** No explicit trauma content reported, but heightened fear warrants monitoring.  
- **Suicidality / Safety:** Explicit self‑harm thoughts → immediate safety concern.  

---

### 4. Highlighted Risk Factors
- **Persistent dysphoria:** Sadness, loss of pleasure, crying several times weekly.  
- **Sleep impairment:** Insomnia/fragmented sleep contributing to fatigue.  
- **Feelings of worthlessness/guilt:** Self‑blame regarding parenting adequacy.  
- **Anxiety & panic:** Unexplained worry and fear, especially about infant safety.  
- **Overwhelming stress:** Perceived inability to cope with daily tasks.  
- **Suicidal ideation:** Direct endorsement of self‑harm thoughts → **Flagged as acute safety risk**.

---

### 5. Screening Observation Summary
The client endorses multiple core symptoms consistent with postpartum depression and anxiety, including marked anhedonia, pervasive sadness, excessive guilt, heightened anxiety/panic, overwhelming stress, and significant sleep disturbance. The presence of recurrent crying and impaired functioning further underscores clinical severity. Notably, the client reports thoughts of self‑harm, which constitutes an immediate safety concern requiring urgent risk assessment and appropriate crisis intervention. No formal diagnosis is rendered at this stage; however, the symptom profile warrants comprehensive psychiatric evaluation and safety planning.
